title: G. Gabrielle StarrFeeling Beauty: The Neuroscience of Aesthetic ExperienceFeeling Beauty: The Neuroscience of Aesthetic Experience. G. Gabrielle Starr. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2013. Pp. viii+259.
abstract: Previous articleNext article FreeBook ReviewG. Gabrielle Starr Feeling Beauty: The Neuroscience of Aesthetic Experience Feeling Beauty: The Neuroscience of Aesthetic Experience. G. Gabrielle Starr. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2013. Pp. viii+259.Lucy HartleyLucy HartleyUniversity of Michigan Search for more articles by this author PDFPDF PLUSFull Text Add to favoritesDownload CitationTrack CitationsPermissionsReprints Share onFacebookTwitterLinked InRedditEmailQR Code SectionsMoreSince the 1990s, a growing body of work in literary studies has sought to explain the processes of reading, appreciation, and evaluation by recourse to scientific theories of mind. This “cognitive turn” in literary studies could be seen, in part, as a development from earlier work on the relationship between science and literature pioneered by Gillian Beer and George Levine and, in part, as a response to debates about the value of—and crisis in—the humanities. It is notable, for instance, that a number of the leading proponents of cognitive approaches to literature are (or were originally) specialists in the fields of eighteenth-century, Romantic, and nineteenth-century literature.1 And yet the conjunction of neuroscience, cognitive science, and the humanities has produced a capacious field of inquiry, which ranges across historical periods for its examples and uses different theories of mind to explore how we feel, what we can know about the creative world, and why it matters.From the title alone, it is clear that G. Gabrielle Starr’s new book will take up the opportunity to explore the connections between feeling and knowing from the broad perspective of aesthetic experience, that is, our emotional responses to beauty in art and in nature. Feeling Beauty, however, is distinctive in both presenting new research on the regions of the brain activated by intense aesthetic responses and suggesting the ways in which this research might open up a new, dynamic understanding of aesthetics. One point of reference for the book is obviously Alexander Baumgarten’s introduction of the term “aesthetics” in 1735 to designate a science of sensory cognition.2 Another, perhaps less obvious, is Semir Zeki’s coining of the term “neuroaesthetics” in the late 1990s to register the importance of understanding aesthetic experiences in relation to the mechanisms of the brain.3 These are historically distant points, but Starr brings them together by presenting her work as a contribution to the unfinished project of learning more about aesthetics that, in turn, raises issues related to how we experience beauty, sublimity, awe, and fear. In a refreshingly straightforward style, she explains how an experimental study of aesthetic experience, conducted at New York University’s Center for Brain Imaging by Edward A. Vessel, Nava Rubin, and Starr, provides evidence for the claims advanced in Feeling Beauty.4 The introduction and first chapter outline the importance of neuroaesthetics as an interpretive model for understanding emotion, pleasure, and reward in the sister arts (visual art, music, and literature), while the second chapter argues for motor imagery as the functional basis for aesthetic experience (including visual imagery), and the third chapter suggests some applications of a fluid, variable, and layered perspective on the arts and some possible avenues for future inquiry.Feeling Beauty is a short book, despite its broad subject, but it contains a number of fascinating insights into brain responses to the sister arts, the differences between aesthetic experience and ordinary emotion, and the neural systems activated by the most intense responses to artworks. The central premise is that “aesthetic experience relies on a distributed neural architecture, a set of brain areas involved in emotion, perception, imagery, memory, and language,” and that it “emerges from networked interactions, the workings of intricately connected and coordinated brain systems that, together, form a flexible architecture enabling us to develop new arts and to see the world around us differently” (xv). Thus construed, Starr’s aim is to distinguish between our emotional responses to the arts and our ordinary emotional responses to, say, faces and landscapes in order to offer a “testable hypothesis (in scientific terms) and a theory (in humanist terms) of experiences of art across multiple domains” (30). The most intriguing and original part of the book is, I think, the argument that intense aesthetic responses are events, which occur when areas of the brain that are usually active during waking rest and deactivated with external stimuli become engaged by artworks. Starr demonstrates how the activation of what is called the default mode network makes aesthetic responses distinctive because they are not predictable and they are not essential for survival but, rather, depend on surprise, variation, and competition. Her claim is that “reward itself is not enough to distinguish aesthetic response, nor is it enough to identify what is different about arresting experience”; instead, “either the default mode network may integrate computational reward into a complex experience of emotions and intense aesthetic feeling or, perhaps more likely, its engagement may signify that such an integration has taken place” (64).The implications of these ideas need to be worked out through more scientific research and experimentation, as Starr readily admits. Nevertheless, she offers a preliminary guide to their relevance for the humanities by focusing on how aesthetic experience constitutes a “restructuring of value” that leads not “to new ‘facts’” but “new configurations of knowledge” (15). Because this book is intentionally open ended, a sort of prospectus for further research, it raises more questions than it can answer about the new kinds of knowledge and new structures of value supplied by aesthetic experience. This is no bad thing nor is it surprising as the book is, at once, a scientifically grounded study of aesthetic experience and a series of speculations about new ways of understanding aesthetics. The result, in my opinion, is that the scientific dimensions of the book, supported by results from the New York University study, seemed to outweigh the humanistic dimensions, illustrated primarily by examples from the eighteenth century, including Immanuel Kant, Johann Winckelmann, William Hogarth, John Dryden, and John Keats, though also including Ovid, Elizabeth Bishop, Gian Lorenzo Bernini and the Elgin Marbles, Ludwig van Beethoven, Vincent Van Gogh, and Jackson Pollock. Indeed, I found Starr’s analysis of poetry according to neuroaesthetic ideas more compelling than her interpretations of visual art, which led me to wonder whether the scientific evidence deriving from a controlled experiment might have been more fruitfully explored through fewer, more detailed, examples from the arts. Furthermore, I would have liked to hear Starr elaborate on the contrast she draws between a neuroscientific model of aesthetic experience and the understanding of aesthetics presented by evolutionary psychologists. Granted, Starr wants to avoid “mapping the phenomena of aesthetic experience onto basic evolutionary drives” (27); however, she raises the possibility that aesthetic experience might have an adaptive function, which would be worth pursuing in the light of the claim made for aesthetic responses as transient events that nonetheless produce changes in “how we think and feel in the now…and in the future” (147). All of this is to say that I wanted to learn more about how a neural approach might prompt us to rethink aesthetic experience.The application of neurological and cognitive theories to literature and the arts is not without its detractors: it is sometimes seen as a reductive approach to the diversity of literary and other art forms, and sometimes as an imposition of twenty-first century ideas on the thoughts and feelings expressed in earlier historical periods. By and large, Feeling Beauty avoids these sorts of criticism, for Starr carefully describes the process at work in the brain without diminishing their complexity or foreclosing their possible applications to the humanities. There is still much work to be done in explaining aesthetic experience, work that I hope G. Gabrielle Starr will continue through collaboration and experimentation because I learned a lot from her study of Feeling Beauty—and I look forward to learning more in the future.Notes1 I am thinking here of Alan Richardson, British Romanticism and the Science of Mind (Cambridge University Press, 2001), and The Neural Sublime: Cognitive Theories and Romantic Texts (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2010); Lisa Zunshine, Why We Read Fiction: Theory of Mind and the Novel (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2006); Blakey Vermeule, The Party of Humanity: Writing Moral Psychology in Eighteenth-Century Britain (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2000), and Why Do We Care about Literary Characters? (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 2009); Kay Young, Imagining Minds: The Neuro-Aesthetics of Austen, Eliot, and Hardy (Columbus: Ohio State University Press, 2010); and Anne Stiles, Popular Fiction and Brain Science in the Late Nineteenth Century (Cambridge University Press, 2012).2 Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten, Reflections on Poetry: Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten’s “Meditationes philosophicae de nonnullis ad poema pertinentibus,” trans. Karl Aschenbrenner and William B. Holther (1735; Berkeley: University of California Press, 1954).3 Semir Zeki, “The Woodhull Lecture: Visual Art and the Visual Brain,” Proceedings of the Royal Institution of Great Britain 68 (1997): 29–63, Inner Vision: An Exploration of Art and the Brain (Oxford University Press, 1999), and “Artistic Creativity and the Brain,” Science 293 (2001): 51–52. See also the Institute of Neuroesthetics at http://www.neuroesthetics.org/institute.php.4 The results of this study were published in Edward A. Vessel, G. Gabrielle Starr, and Nava Rubin, “The Brain on Art: Intense Aesthetic Experience Activates the Default Mode Network,” Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 6:66 (2012), doi:10:3389/fnhum.2012.00066. An excerpt from the article is included as the appendix to Feeling Beauty, 151–57; further investigation can be found in Edward A. Vessel, G. Gabrielle Starr, and Nava Rubin, “Art Reaches Within: Aesthetic Experience, the Self, and the Default Mode Network,” Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 7:258 (2013), doi:10.3389/fnins.2013.00258. title: The Life and Crimes of Doris Payne
abstract: Video: The Life and Crimes of Doris Payne (72 Min) Co-producers and Directors: Matthew Pond and Kirk Marcolina Released: 2013 Distributed by CinemaGuild: http://www.cinemaguild.com/ The Life and Crimes of Doris Payne is a stylish, engrossing, and ultimately sad film about an 84-year-old Black American woman who achieved fame and notoriety as a world-class jewel thief in a career that spans 64 years. In the opening and closing scenes of the video, Doris, then 80 years old, is accused of stealing an $8,000 diamond ring from a Macy’s store in San Diego. How did this amiable, soft-spoken old woman get into this situation? The film relates her life story—or more correctly—life episodes within a life course perspective, recruiting her friends, family members, law enforcement, a college professor, and primarily Doris herself to share their views of her roots, motives, methods, morals, and continuing recidivism. The Rorschach-like telling allows viewers to draw their own answers to the question: Who is Doris Payne? How did “a poor, single, African-American mother from segregated 1930’s America wind up as one of the world’s most notorious and successful jewel thieves?” ( http://dorispaynefilm.com/dorispaynefilm.com/The_Film.html ) ( Figure 1 ). Doris Payne, age 80. When Doris was in her early teens, a jewelry store owner threw her out of his shop when he saw a white customer entering the store. Doris: “He didn’t want another customer to see him treating a black person in kind fashion. I used to cry about it. I felt like I was just nothing.” After this incident, she began to enter stores, take a piece of jewelry, stop at the exit, and shout back, “You forgot this one” to taunt and to embarrass the shop keepers. Stealing jewelry became “a necessity” when her father’s abuse of her mother “began to be bloody.” She stole her first diamond in Pittsburgh and gave her mother the cash to get out of town. She stuck with it when she saw how easy it was to do; consequently, she got very good at it. Doris: It was “. . . exciting. It became a social outlet for me. That was my everything . I could be anybody I wanted to be for a minute – a socialite, American, European, a nurse.” Richard Yarborough, Professor of English at UCLA, believes that Doris’ actions have historical precedent as a trickster : “The trickster is a folk hero in African-American history who achieves his or her ends through deception, through masking. The victory of the trickster is measured by the trickster’s ability to ridicule the person in authority”—most of whom have higher social status. Yarborough sees Doris receiving a great deal of satisfaction and amusement from some of her adventures. She tells the videographers that she loved playing multiple roles. Doris recalls that when she was portraying the rich society matron, purveyors did not see her as a Black American woman: “I’ve had many, many people just say to me, ‘Oh you’re not Black. You don’t act Black’.” Doris’ daughter sees her as a pioneer for women’s rights: “She obviously saw herself as a single-minded woman who could do what she wanted to do when she wanted to do it during a time when women were still trying to figure it out. That’s what’s fabulous about it.” Doris’ methods are as intriguing as her motives, revealing her intimate knowledge about creating expectations of trustworthiness that allow her steal without difficulty. Her techniques are shown via re-enactments. In her socialite role, she dresses in expensive clothing and jewelry. Jewelers spread several pieces of jewelry on a countertop in front of her. A friend explains that Doris “then starts her slight of hand game, moving them around, wearing them, moving them around at a dizzying pace. Then distracting the sales clerk, who’ll look away, she grabs one. She’ll then ask where that particular piece is. As they look about for the jewelry, Doris will then ‘discover it’ and give it back to the jeweler. ‘Here it is.’ She earns the trust of the jeweler. ‘Oh, she’s trustworthy’.” Over time, her “campaigns” (as she calls them) turned to the international arena. Doris states that she preferred Europe because Europeans have a focus on proper behavior and correct attire, which she could easily enact. She used jewelry ads published in Town and Country Magazine to target her stores. She generated huge revenue from jewel thefts in London, Rome, Milan, Paris, Belgium, and Switzerland (where she once escaped custody by jumping from a train). Motivated by the Hitchcock film “To Catch a Thief” about a master jewel thief operating in Monte Carlo, Doris was excited to try her craft in the principality. She stole a large diamond ring from a Monte Carlo shop, her largest theft. The price on the tag was followed by nine zeros. She had violated the cardinal rule of the profession—stealing something “too big.” She was arrested and received a 3-year sentence. She claims that authorities never found the ring. Her success with these higher level targets brought her world-wide fame and placed her permanently on the international law enforcement list of “usual suspects” (e.g., Figure 2 ). Doris Payne, age 36. A number of age-related issues emerge in The Life and Times of Doris Payne that have relevance for gerontologists as well as life course educators. The very uniqueness of her unusual life scenario underscores the importance of recognizing the social and psychological diversity that exist among older adults. As an “outlier” in the area of crime and the elderly, Doris’ case entices us to move beyond our usual stereotypes of elders as victims to consider the meanings that aging has for criminal recidivists who survive to old age. In particular, it challenges us to reconsider what productive aging may mean for elders who are socially and legally labeled as “counter-productive.” Doris’ notoriety is couched in a romanticism of respect for the stealth of the fox, which she embraces. Doris: “I’m exceptionally proud of being opposite of what is expected. I’m glad it was a Black woman that did it.” Lifespan developmentalists and geropsychologists may also find the film of interest. For example, on the surface, her life-long career of thievery seems to support a continuity perspective on personality. However, her reasons for continuing her stealing, if we can trust her reports, vary as a function of her changing needs across her life course (e.g., stealing to support her mother versus stealing because of an addictive excitement factor—a pattern that nicely illustrates Gordon Allport’s theory of the functional autonomy of motives ( http://psycnet.apa.org/books/11305/008 ). The film raises (but does not directly address) questions about the relation of the ontogeny of development and aging to antisocial behavior. For example, though she reports that her thievery satisfied different psychological needs at different phases in her life course, we are left to wonder if her lifelong pattern of behavior is overridden or fixed by antisocial personality disorder? Doris’ behavior seems “frozen in time.” Does this behavioral rigidity indicate a corresponding developmental fixation? If not how has her psychosocial development changed across her lifespan? How do developmental changes influence the subtle shifts we see in Doris’ behavior in later life? Older Doris has abandoned her larger campaigns of her younger years. Her thefts in recent years seem more spontaneous, with a greater sense of immediacy, now targeting smaller and more local shops. Older Doris is more fearful of the prison environment, of its negative impact on her health. Older Doris no longer embraces the view that imprisonment is just part of her criminal lifestyle, a part of the “game.” Older Doris now lives in a different era, preceded by her notoriety and a new age of highly sophisticated security technology. At the conclusion of her Macy’s trial, Doris’ lawyer asks the Judge to appreciate that “there’s more to Doris Payne” than her criminal behavior. The Judge responds: “She’s a thief. She has a nice way about her, a nice manner which she used to exploit her relationship [with the jeweler]. She’s charming. She’s Santa Claus’ wife. That’s who she is. There’s more to her than her 32 aliases? There’s more to her than her 10 different dates of birth. There’s more to her than her 11 Social Security numbers. Nine names on passports?” He sentenced her to 5 years for the Macy’s crime. She was released after 2½ years due to prison overcrowding. The Life and Crimes of Doris Payne allows viewers to construct their own answers to the question: Who is Doris Payne ? Most people experience life within the shaping limits of their intellect and personalities, and the passage of time. Most are able to form deep attachments, a stable moral compass, distinguish between truth and falsehood, learn from their mistakes, feel guilt or remorse, and empathize with and nurture others. In my view, there is an ultimate sadness in the fact Doris Payne lacks these capacities , though the film does not share much about her role as a mother. To a large extent, she has been a life-long prisoner of her own antisocial personality tendencies, a classic example of the “catch me if you can” sociopath . Beyond and behind this label, however, much about Doris remains inchoate.

title: Hegel, moderniste? Remarks on Robert Pippin's After the Beautiful
abstract: Robert Pippin's After the Beautiful presents a case for the continuing relevance of Hegel's aesthetic theory and of more broadly Hegelian approaches to the philosophy of art.1 As is characteristic of Pippin's work, the book is both illuminating and a rich source for further reflection. Pippin's case relies on restricting certain of Hegel's philosophical views, and the restrictions in question are not trivial. In particular, Hegel's claim that art no longer can have a leading or even significant role in increased human self‐understanding and in the realization of freedom must be set aside (pp. 35–39). Such negative pronouncements on the part of Hegel concerning art's continued viability for modern European self‐understanding simply have not stood the test of time. So, Pippin holds that, going forward, the Hegelian should treat such attitudes on the part of Hegel as extrusions of an overly strict, teleological conception of dialectic. One must liberate Hegelianism, that is, from the letter of Hegel's dialectic and so from his statements that art has ended—first, with respect to its role as a leading vehicle of human self‐knowledge in classical Greece and, second, in terms of its very ability to convey further self‐knowledge with romanticism. Divorcing dialectic from overarching teleology is in effect the only Hegelian thing to do if Hegel's dialectical conception of self‐determination (Selbstbestimmung) is to gain purchase in the discussion of modern art. More specifically Pippin is concerned to understand in Hegelian terms modern European painting roughly from the realism of Courbet and Manet to post‐impressionism. Pippin refers to this as a period of “pictorial modernism.” I take it that this phrase is to be understood as an abbreviated genitive that one should read both “subjectively” and “objectively.” That is, pictorial modernism is both the modernism of pictorial art (genitivus obiectivus = how modernism is expressed via the pictorial arts) and a specific kind of modernism (genitivus subiectivus = how modernism more generally is pictorial). Although Pippin does not quite come out and say it, After the Beautiful forwards a competitor to the mainstream way of charting the development of modern pictorial art (and other modern art as well) in terms of its increasing musicality. This conception of the development of art in the period under consideration, which one finds in different forms in Schelling, Schopenhauer, Wagner, Nietzsche, and Adorno, is a species of the Renaissance practice of paragone, taking the move from figural art to abstraction to be more indicative of what counts as “modern.” But it is not exactly silent on Pippin's favorite examples of French realism. It is important to note that the musicality hypothesis is compatible with certain aspects of Hegel's aesthetic progressivism, for instance, with the idea that one mode of art goads inferior modes into replicating imperfectly the advanced effects and structures of the superior mode. So, I am not sure Pippin wants to reject the musicality thesis outright and replace it with his concentration on pictorial modernism as a leading edge or whether he holds that they can complement one another. Prima facie the contrast between the two ways of thinking about modern art promises to be stark. For the musicality theorist the central concern is releasing subjectivity from the normative confines of the social and natural world through procedures of figural abstraction and summoning forth the Dionysian unconscious. The subjectivity primarily at issue here is not one pre‐adapted to sociality but rather one that increases its depth by radically restructuring reality in its own terms. This project has its clear antecedents in romanticism, as many scholars have recognized. In contrast, Pippin's Hegel will valorize realism—a position the historical Hegel would certainly have appreciated—and the idea of mutual recognition, not a breaking of the social vessels, is central. So, while Pippin is careful to restrict his specific case for the continuing relevance of Hegel's philosophy of art to the time period extending from what many art historians take to be the emergence of modern painting in Manet in the 1860s to the stirrings of figural abstraction in Cézanne's Bathers from the first decade of the twentieth century, there is even more at stake. Hegel of course did not live to see modern Europe. If one were to take as authoritative Hegel's statements at the conclusion of his lectures on aesthetics, one would not have much to go on in developing an account of modernism. One would be left with an extension of Dutch portraiture or with what Hegel calls in his treatment of poetry “true” or “objective” humor.2 It is my sense that Pippin takes his cue very much from the former. The latter is not a very exciting category by modernist lights.3 How one moves on from Hegel in a yet recognizably Hegelian vein raises questions both of (A) whether one can isolate sufficiently the results of the dialectic from the teleological dialectical apparatus and (B) if one can do so, which elements of dialectic one would feature going forward. I agree with Pippin that Hegel's own view generally is that Geist is in a position to certify to itself that it has achieved in principle full reconciliation with aspects of the world, it, and the relation of world to it, that were otherwise alienating. Hegel makes this claim for theoretical closure at a level of philosophical analysis that he considers much more advanced than the consideration of art—that is, at the level of the final and culminating form of what he calls “Absolute Spirit,” that is, “Philosophy.” “Art” is also a form of Absolute Spirit, one that is subordinate to Philosophy, and the impact of full reconciliation and theoretical closure on it follows from the subordination. Art's “end” for Hegel is, in that sense, a technical result internal to Hegel's theory of Absolute Spirit. Pippin does not argue for (A) above but finds himself in a long line of neo‐Hegelians in holding that releasing the teleological constraints of Hegel's own conception of dialectic as they operate at the overarching architectonic level does not present any special problem with preserving a recognizably Hegelian conception of dialectical rationality. He is also in neo‐Hegelian company in answering (B), in finding the conception of recognition to be a key to advancing “what lives,” as Croce put it, of Hegel.4 What is required to advance Hegel's views into modernity is a sense of recognition with ample room for alienation, that is, what one might call a Hegelian sense of failed recognition. And that is precisely what Pippin provides. Before one gets to the topic of recognition, two preliminary matters of reconstruction seem crucial for Pippin. The first is to preserve Hegel's historicism, especially as it intersects with another element of his thought: his rejection of a strict concept/percept division. Hegel treats the concept/percept binary contextually. The binary is theoretically permissible and even necessary and progressive given certain background assumptions. But if one were to ask whether ultimately there is a divide in theory or experience between categorial thought and cognitive receptivity, the answer for Hegel clearly would be that there is no such division. Second, Hegel analyzes action as a full‐fledged and, in many ways, basic form of thought. In particular, bodily action of forming objects is thinking, as is the bodily action of forming things whose main point is that they be seen as expressing the action constitutive of their making—for instance, art. It is worthwhile at this point to step back from Hegel's own doctrines in order to motivate via a more neutral medium how they might be extended in the artistic cases Pippin discusses. Hegel views art as inherently dealing in sensuously embedded concepts. That art is conceptual means that it is a form of Geist’s self‐expression and self‐knowledge; that it is sensuous is what makes it the form of Absolute Spirit that it is over and against other such forms. What is at issue here is visual art and sight; more specifically, what is at stake is how sight might be a form of conceptual life. Now, there is an approach to perception when it comes to considering sense modalities and their relation to more articulating modes of cognition that holds that sense modalities an sich and at their basic level are impervious to conceptual articulation. Sensuous perception on this account is passive in its receptivity, and whatever role it has in conceptually articulated experience is given to it “down the line” by higher order, conceptual modes of experience: one can and does (quite a lot of the time) see without thinking. But this is not the only approach to perception. One might instead argue that seeing is dependent on looking. To say that seeing is dependent on looking is to say that to see X one needs to orient one's sight with regard to X—that is, that seeing X requires an intentional action of bringing sight to X. Given this, one might informally summarize an argument for the ascription of recognition at a pre‐predicative or pre‐reflective level of visual experience as follows: Looking is an intentional activity, that is, one which operates even at the point of its minimal specification in terms of something like “choice.” Intentional activities, even at minimal levels of their specifications, are already cognitively structured and, so, are pre‐adapted to further structuring by intentional content of a more developed sort (for instance, beliefs). Seeing requires looking. Seeing is always intentional. Seeing, because intentional itself, is pre‐adapted to structuring in terms of more developed intentional content. I believe Hegel would accept something like this account of vision and its relation to looking and its inherent conceptual articulation, and I take it that Pippin would agree (pp. 41–42, 49–50). The conclusion of the argument is compatible with treating perception as embodied; Merleau‐Ponty is a kind of Hegelian in this sense. It is also compatible with treating the conceptual articulation of perceptual states as a matter of the concepts that are available for such structuring at different points in history. That said, it is easy to see that, while the argument establishes a potential basis for grafting the structure of Hegelian recognition to pre‐reflective visual states that form the basis for an aesthetic, sensuous dimension, by itself it is insufficient to do so. It is simply not specific enough. For one thing, from the fact that seeing involves looking and from the fact that looking involves at least some minimal sense of regard for the thing looked at, one cannot draw any immediate conclusion concerning whether such regard will be positive, negative, or in between. Even assuming that what is looked at is another looker, that does not without more entail that the regard is a kind of recognition, which in the Hegelian vein is certainly not neutral and in most cases operates according to at least a tacit ideal of positive mutual regard. (Of course, in some of the most famous of his cases, Hegel attempts to show that mutual antagonistic regard is the product of at least the stirrings of, say, respect.) Nor does the conclusion of the argument entail that the regard, be it positive or negative, would provide an impetus to sustained interaction between one who is looking, on the one hand, and what or whom is being looked at, on the other. That the thing looked at is itself a looker also does not guarantee this result without more said about the relation of looking, the nature of lookers, or both. But here again it seems that ordinary experience can help the Hegelian out a bit, for looking and being looked at do seem to be basically experientially and conceptually interrelated. Soon after a child can look she is aware that she can be looked at, and this awareness infiltrates and forms her looking in terms of her being looked at. This is a signal structure for the Hegelian, as Pippin emphasizes, for the reciprocity of seeing qua looking now can be further specified in terms of recognition and its application to at least visual art that makes the combination of looking and being looked at thematic, and some modernist visual art clearly has that brief. For, once one allows that seeing has intentional structure ab initio, it is open to one to argue that this intentional base can be modeled in various sorts of personal, social, and historical ways by interpenetrating conceptual resources. That is, the idea of intention here plays a structural role within an account of perception that facilitates what one might call the reciprocal ‘travel’ of cognitive resources from the more generically articulated to the less and from the less to the more. As Pippin writes in the introductory sections of the book, this picture is implied but not very well worked out by Kant (pp. 9–15); Hegel's epistemology makes it central by emphasizing the importance of the historical constitution of such resources.5 Of course, none of this structure uniquely supports the progressive historical story Hegelians often tell about such resources or the idea that reconciliation is always a tacit ideal of recognition. Hegelians will have to argue for the merits of those ideas independently. This is the point at which recognition can reenter the story. Ordinarily recognition is an explicit and fully conceptual action; one would not ordinarily say that seeing without more involves the sort of regard that typifies Hegelian recognition. “Recognition” is a social–moral category for him that, if it has work to do at the perceptual/sensuous level, will involve various relatively conceptually inarticulate ways of looking and being looked at. Take Manet's Olympia. The painting is both a mediation and provocation concerning canons of looking at nudes. The titular figure looks at one looking at her as a nude; her look says, depending on one's interpretation, “what are you looking at?” “what are you looking at?” or “why are looking at all?”6 Her look defies that of the onlooker, thereby placing in question the art‐historical project of making objects that solicit the kinds of looking that female nudes typically do. T. J. Clark's treatment of the Olympia and of other of Manet's works strikes me as especially convincing.7 As Clark sees things, the painting is in dialogue with both the historical practice of painting nudes (compare Manet's reference to Titian's Venus of Urbino) as well as with the “low” material culture of its day. Michael Fried has argued that one such source is the contemporary practice of photographing prostitutes for pornographic purposes.8 Alexander Nehamas extends the point in holding that the painting is of such a photographic session.9 Nehamas's more explicit reference to photography overreaches; it is more plausible and powerful to view Manet's painting as painting not of a photographic session but under the aesthetic style of such photography, as Fried suggests. Nevertheless, concentration on photography as a normative presence in the work is brilliant in unmasking the particular kind of pretention that Olympia's look foregrounds. Its focus on the encroachment of exchange relations (prostitutes, pornographic postcards) into easel painting is of a piece with Clark's insistence that, if one looks hard enough at scenes of middle‐ and lower middle‐class leisure painted in impressionism, one sees factories and other modes of advancing industrialization. For Clark, the appeal to “flatness” that features, say, in Greenberg's account of abstract expressionism and Fry's of post‐impressionism gains in social weight in Manet's case; the flatness of the canvas is a very specific sort—the flatness of such photographs. One tries to look at Olympia under the duplicitous guise of the nude—as if looking at her were anything but buying her for erotic use. Her look at that looking—the way being looked at is directed back at the audience—disabuses one of the fiction. She does not merely look at or past one; rather she looks through one. title: Naturalism in the Theatre (Émile Zola)
abstract: EACH WINTER AT THE beginning of the theatre season I fall prey to the same thoughts. A hope springs up in me, and I tell myself that before the first warmth of summer empties the playhouses, a dramatist of genius will be discovered. Our theatre desperately needs a new man who will scour the debased boards and bring about a rebirth in an art degraded by its practitioners to the simple-minded requirements of the crowd. Yes, it would take a powerful personality, an innovator’s mind, to overthrow the accepted conventions and finally install the real human drama in place of the ridiculous untruths that are on display today. I picture this creator scorning the tricks of the clever hack, smashing the imposed patterns, remaking the stage until it is continuous with the auditorium, giving a shiver of life to the painted trees, letting in through the backcloth the great, free air of reality. Unfortunately, this dream I have every October has not yet been fulfilled, and is not likely to be for some time. I wait in vain, I go from failure to failure. Is this, then, merely the naive wish of a poet? Are we trapped in today’s dramatic art, which is so confining, like a cave that lacks air and light? Certainly, if dramatic art by its nature forbids this escape into less restricted forms, it would indeed be vain to delude ourselves and to expect a renaissance at any moment. But despite the stubborn assertions of certain critics who do not like to have their standards threatened, it is obvious that dramatic art, like all the arts, has before it an unlimited domain, without barriers of any kind to left or right. Inability, human incapacity, is the only boundary to an art. To understand the need for a revolution in the theatre, we must establish clearly where we stand today. During our entire classical period tragedy ruled as an absolute monarch. It was rigid and intolerant, never granting its subjects a touch of freedom, bending the greatest minds to its inexorable laws. If a playwright tried to break away from them he was condemned as witless, incoherent and bizarre; he was almost considered a dangerous man. Yet even within the narrow formula genius did build its monument of marble and bronze. The formula was born during the Greek and Latin revival; the artists who took it over found in it a pattern that would serve for great works. Only later, when the imitators – that line of increasingly weaker and punier disciples – came along, did the faults in the formula show up: outlandish situations, improbabilities, dishonest uniformity, and uninterrupted, unbearable declaiming. Tragedy maintained such a sway that two hundred years had to pass before it went out of date. It tried slowly to become more flexible, but without success, for the authoritarian principles in which it was grounded formally forbade any concession to new ideas, under pain of death. Just when it was trying to broaden its scope, it was overturned, after a long and glorious reign. In the eighteenth century romantic drama was already stirring inside tragedy. On occasion the three unities were violated, more importance was given to scenery and extras, violent climaxes were now staged, where formerly they had been described in speeches so that the majestic tranquillity of psychological analysis might not be disturbed by physical action. In addition, the passion of the grande époque was replaced by commonplace acting; a grey rain of mediocrity and staleness soaked the stage. One can visualize tragedy, by the beginning of this century, as a long, pale, emaciated figure without a drop of blood under its white skin, trailing its tattered robes across a gloomy stage on which the footlights had gone dark of their own accord. A rebirth of dramatic art out of a new formula was inevitable. It was then that romantic drama noisily planted its standard in front of the prompter’s box. The hour had come; a slow ferment had been at work; the insurrection advanced on to terrain already softened-up for the victory. And never has the word insurrection seemed more apt, for romantic drama bodily seized the monarch tragedy and, out of hatred for its impotence, sought to destroy every memory of its reign. Tragedy did not react; it sat still on its throne, guarding its cold majesty, persisting with its speeches and descriptions. Whereas romantic drama made action its rule, excesses of action that leapt to the four corners of the stage, hitting out to right and left, no longer reasoning or analysing, giving the public a full view of the blood-drenched horror of its climaxes. Tragedy had chosen antiquity for its setting, the eternal Greeks and Romans, immobilizing the action in a room or in front of the columns of a temple; romantic drama chose the Middle Ages, paraded knights and ladies, manufactured strange sets with castles pinnacled over sheer gorges, armories crowded with weapons, dungeons dripping with moisture, ancient forests pocked with moonlight. The war was joined on all fronts; romantic drama ruthlessly made itself the armed adversary of tragedy and assaulted it with every method that defied the old formula. This raging hostility, which characterized the romantic drama at its high tide, needs to be stressed, for it o»ers a precious insight. The poets who led the movement undoubtedly talked about putting real passion on stage and laying claim to a vast new realm that would encompass the whole of human life with its contradictions and inconsistencies; it is worth remembering, for example, that romantic drama fought above all for a mixture of laughter and tears in the same play, arguing that joy and pain walk side by side on earth. Yet truth, reality, in fact counted for little – even displeased the innovators. They had only one passion, to overthrow the tragic formula that inhibited them, to crush it once and for all under a stampede of every kind of audacity. They did not want their heroes of the Middle Ages to be more real than the heroes of tragic antiquity; they wanted them to appear as passionate and splendid as their predecessors had appeared cold and correct. A mere skirmish over dress and modes of speech, nothing more: one set of puppets at odds with another. Togas were torn up in favour of doublets; a lady, instead of addressing her lover as ‘My lord’, called him ‘My lion’. After the transition fiction still prevailed; only the setting was di»erent. I do not want to be unfair to the romantic movement. Its e»ect has been outstanding and unquestionable; it has made us what we are: free artists. It was, I repeat, a necessary revolution, a violent struggle that arose just in time to sweep away a tragic convention that had become childish. Still, it would be ridiculous to arrest the evolution of dramatic art at romanticism. These days, especially, it is astounding to read certain prefaces in which the 1830 movement is announced as the triumphal entry into human truth. Our forty-year distance is enough to let us see clearly that the alleged truth of the romanticists is a persistent and monstrous exaggeration of reality, a fantasy that has declined into excesses. Tragedy, to be sure, is another type of falseness, but it is not more false. Between the characters who pace about in togas, endlessly discussing their passions with confidants, and the characters in doublets who perform great feats and flit about like insects drunk with the sun, there is nothing to choose; both are equally and totally unacceptable. Such people have never existed. Romantic heroes are only tragic heroes bitten by the mardi gras bug, hiding behind false noses, and dancing the dramatic cancan after drinking. For the old sluggish rhetoric the 1830 movement substituted an excited, full-blooded rhetoric, and that is all. Without believing that art progresses, we can still say that it is continuously in motion, among all civilizations, and that this motion reflects di»erent phases of the human mind. Genius is made manifest in every formula, even in the most primitive and innocent ones, though the formulas become transmuted according to the intellectual breadth of each civilization; that is incontestable. If Aeschylus was great, Shakespeare and Molière showed themselves to be equally great, each within his di»ering civilization and formula. By this I mean that I set apart the creative genius who knows how to make the most of the formula of his time. There is no progress in human creation but there is a logical succession to the formulas, to methods of thought and expression. Thus, art takes the same strides as humanity, is its very language, goes where it goes, moves with it towards light and truth; but for that, we could never judge whether a creator’s e»orts were more or less great, depending on whether he comes at the beginning or end of a literature. In these terms, it is certain that when we left tragedy behind, the romantic drama was a first step in the direction of the naturalistic drama, towards which we are now advancing. The romantic drama cleared the ground, proclaimed the freedom of art. Its love of action, its mixture of laughter and tears, its research into accuracy of costume and setting show the movement’s impulse towards real life. Is this not how things happen during every revolution against a secular regime? One begins by breaking windows, chanting and shouting, wrecking relics of the last regime with hammer blows. There is a first exuberance, an intoxication with the new horizons faintly glimpsed, excesses of all kinds that go beyond the original aims and degenerate into the despotism of the old, hated system, those very abuses the revolution has just fought against. In the heat of the battle tomorrow’s truths evaporate. And not until all is calm and the fever has abated is there any regret for the broken windows, any understanding of how the e»ort has gone awry, how the new laws have been prematurely thrown together so that they are hardly any improvement over the laws that were destroyed. Well, the whole history of romantic drama is there. It may have been the formula necessary for its time, it may have had truthful intuitions, it may have been the form that will always be celebrated because a great poet used it to compose his masterpieces. At the present time it is, none the less, a ridiculous, outdated formula, with a rhetoric that o»ends us. We now wonder why it was necessary to push in windows, wave swords, bellow without a break, to go a scale too shrill in sentiment and language. All that leaves us cold, it bores and annoys us. Our condemnation of the romantic formula is summed up in one severe remark: To destroy one rhetoric it was not necessary to invent another. Today, then, tragedy and romantic drama are equally old and worn out. And that is hardly to the credit of the latter, it should be said, for in less than half a century it has fallen into the same state of decay as tragedy, which took two centuries to die. There it lies, flattened in its turn, overwhelmed by the same passion it showed in its own battle. Nothing is left. We can only guess at what is to come. Logically all that can grow up on that free ground conquered in 1830 is the formula of naturalism.

title: BATTEUX, CHARLES. The Fine Arts Reduced to a Single Principle. Trans. James O. Young. Oxford University Press, 2015, lxxx + 151 pp., $70.00 cloth.
abstract: Charles Batteux (1713–1780) is an important but secondary figure in French enlightenment aesthetics. His primary work, The Fine Arts Reduced to a Single Principle (1746), argues that the imitation of what Batteux calls belle Nature is an underlying principle of all of the fine arts. Batteux is not a systematic thinker in spite of the schematic nature of his work. Exactly what he means by “imitation” and belle Nature is difficult to work out. On the one hand, imitation is a staple of neo‐classical critical theory, and Batteux is conventional in making it the first principle of criticism. On the other hand, he rejects a simple copy theory of imitation. Imitation in the fine arts depends on genius which selects, improves, and transforms nature. Belle Nature remains somewhat obscure, therefore. It is not nature itself or some particular aspect of nature that can be singled out, but it is still the object of imitation. The alternative imaginative projections that emerged in eighteenth‐century pre‐romanticism as the creative product of genius play no role for Batteux. The imagination is almost completely absent in his work. Perhaps the most significant aspect of Batteux's work is its focus on the fine arts. The fine arts taken as a unitary concept emerged from the more craftsmen‐like concepts of the individual arts in the course of the eighteenth century. Batteux is able to take it for granted that there is something called the fine arts, and his claim that what unites painting, poetry, and music is the single principle of imitation is an attempt to establish a critical space for them as fine arts. Because he retains the neo‐classical concept of imitation, however, he has to both stretch it and make it somewhat implausible. Music must have meaning; painting must have human figures; poetry must be selective from nature and have actions. What follows are the rather inconsistent claim that the fine arts produce emotion and “enthusiasm,” and their goal is pleasure, but that nevertheless they are imitations. The specifics of Batteux's theory turn out to be rules, therefore, in typical neo‐classical fashion. Taste plays a role—there is good or bad taste. But taste is rule governed. The variations of taste are relatively insignificant. There is no antinomy of taste or worry about the subjective nature of taste. Batteux writes, “All people are in almost complete agreement in their hearts. … Suppose a man, who has exquisite taste, is attentive to the impact that some work of art has on him, perceives it clearly, and then, as a result, expresses himself. … It is scarcely possible that other people will disagree with his judgements” (p. 34). Batteux differs from neo‐classical theory by giving a more prominent role to pleasure and sentiment—but he still thinks in terms of rules. And while he treats imitation as something more than accurate depiction, an authoritative representation still determines taste. As a consequence, Batteux's actual critical judgments and rules—which occupy the final third of The Fine Arts Reduced to a Single Principle—are quite conventional. “Tragedy imitates the beautiful and great; comedy imitates the ridiculous” (p. 110). “These two arts [painting and poetry] are so similar that in order to have discussed both of them at once, we need only change the names and put ‘painting,’ ‘designing,’ and ‘colouring’ in places of ‘poetry,’ ‘story,’ and ‘versification’” (p. 125). Batteux was, at heart, a neo‐classically trained academic with a love of schematization who, nevertheless, was trying to incorporate and understand the changing artistic landscape with its promotion of the artist and the fine arts to an independent position, and to give a place to the new sentimentalism developed more radically in Britain after the third Earl of Shaftesbury. He is limited but not insignificant in the history of enlightenment aesthetics. James Young provides an extensive introduction to his translation of The Fine Arts as well as detailed notes. The notes are very helpful, almost necessary, because Batteux cites French authors who are likely to be unfamiliar even to specialists in early modern philosophy as well as classical authors. Young identifies each reference and translates the French, Greek, and Latin quotations, which are not always exact. Batteux, as was common in the eighteenth century, often quotes from memory. The notes, therefore, are very useful. Young tries to make the best case possible for the importance of Batteux. He acknowledges Batteux's limited knowledge of philosophy of art, however, and he rightly points out the independence of Batteux from the Abbé Dubos (p. xxvi). What one has, therefore, is a transitional thinker who is incorporating some elements of the new sentimentalism within a traditional neo‐classical framework. Rousseau was attracted to the sentimental elements (p. xxviii) while Diderot was critical of Batteux's obscurity about imitation and belle nature (p. xxix). Young's attempt to show Batteux's importance by linking him to other eighteenth‐century theories of art are not always successful. He finds similarities to Francis Hutcheson's description of beauty as uniformity combined with variety, but they are misleading, I think. Batteux does not have an internal sense theory like Hutcheson's and the appearance of uniformity and variety goes back to common classical sources. The similarities between Hume and Batteux that Young points out are superficial. Batteux's treatment of taste has little relevance to Hume's recognition that the variability of taste demands a standard. Young is quite good in tracing possible connections between Batteux and later German philosophies of the fine art, though what he takes as influences sometimes work against Batteux instead of helping him if one is trying to establish Batteux's importance. In other places, however, he stretches more than the texts will bear. Young tries to recruit Batteux as a forerunner of twentieth‐century aesthetic cognitivism, but this leads him further astray I think. The problem is that earlier twentieth‐century theories of aesthetic experience and neo‐Kantian theories of aesthetic disinterestedness intervene between the mid‐eighteenth‐century critical theories of taste and the cognitive aesthetic theories that Young finds in Batteux as anticipations of more recent cognitive theories. It is true that Batteux understands the fine arts as moral, and that implies that they provide moral knowledge. But when he understands belle nature as implicitly moral, his Catholic/Thomist/Aristotelian assumptions about the good and its relation to the beautiful are at work, and his claims for the morality of the fine arts depend on Horace rather than anticipating recent debates about the knowledge provided by art, which are responses to the separation of art from morality because of its presumed disinterestedness. For Batteux, the fine arts are imitative, moral, and they produce pleasure. The three go together in his mind. One may be able to resolve some of the implicit contradictions in that position by introducing moral pleasure as a kind of knowledge, but Batteux just does not think that deeply. Instead, he gives us the usual platitudes drawn from his favorite classical author, Horace, about instruction through pleasing. Young places a heavy emphasis on Batteux's theory of music as a fine art as one of his significant contributions and hence of his importance. Here too, the case is not completely convincing however. The issue about music is whether what is imitated has meaning. Batteux requires that music have meaning and that it be an imitation. What is imitated is the sound of the voice. The meaning is the emotion. But it does not follow that what is imitated is the meaning. Batteux is actually fairly clear about this. Young confuses the issue when he tries to link Batteux's imitation theory to expression theories of music and emotion by citing research that shows that certain musical patterns typically express certain emotions, a theory that goes back at least to Susanne Langer. Instead, Batteux gets the meaning from the words, which accounts for his primary interest in vocal music. Young recognizes this (p. xlix). For Batteux, music is imitative because, like the words spoken by the voice, the music imitates the sound of the voice and hence reinforces what the words mean. Music gets its meaning from the words, therefore. Batteux's theory of music is of the toe‐tapping, sing‐along variety, not the Susanne Langer emotional expression variety. What remains is Batteux's recognition of a system of the fine arts, and that, not anticipations of subsequent aesthetic theories, gives his work its interest and what importance it has. Rather than attributing the invention of that system to Batteux, as Young sometimes seems to do, however, one would do better to see the system as emergent and credit Batteux with a sometimes confused recognition of what is taking place. That is, in fact, what Batteux himself claims: the fine arts constitute a system because they have a common principle – imitation. Young devotes several pages to the question whether the same arts that Batteux recognizes as fine arts were recognized by the ancients. Batteux largely drops out of the discussion at this point as it focuses on P. O. Kristeller's “The Modern System of the Arts.” But the origin of the concept or system of the fine arts is not really the issue. What Batteux recognizes, however limitedly, is that they are fine arts, and that gives them and the artists who create them a new status. In spite of my reservations about some of the interpretations advocated in the “Introduction,” Young has done the study of early modern aesthetics a significant service. His translation and notes make Batteux's work available in a way that it has not been before. The translation is quite readable. A translator is always faced with difficulties, of course. Young acknowledges that he is not providing a literal translation in all places: “Some passages are extremely opaque. Here a literal translation is of little use. When faced with such passages, I have tried to figure out what Batteux intended to say and I have said it” (p. lxxii). Sometimes he may go a bit too far in an attempt to make the translation colloquial. For example, “Avoient‐ils dessein par se langage emphatique de relever les Arts, & de dérober aux profanes les Mystères des Muses?” becomes “Do they intend by this highfalutin language to elevate the arts and steal the secrets of the muses?” (pp. 15‐16). ‘Highfalutin’ is not exactly what Batteux says, and it jars. In another place “Le Goût est un sentiment,” becomes “Taste, then, is a sense” (p. 31). Given the significance of ‘sentiment’ as a term in eighteenth‐century theories of taste and the fact that elsewhere Young uses the term, it would seem preferable to leave ‘sentiment’ in place and allow the context to determine whether ‘sense,’ which is also a theoretical term in eighteenth‐century aesthetics, is what is meant. No translator can avoid such quibbles, and thanks to the availability of the French original on the internet (for example, https://archive.org/stream/gri_000033125008530772#page/n11/mode/2up) places that seem to raise questions can be consulted. Young's translation of Batteux's The Fine Arts Reduced to a Single Principle is an important addition to the literature, therefore.

title: On German dramaturgy
abstract: In German, the word “dramaturgy” implies two meanings. Following the literal translation of the term from ancient Greek, it means the philosophical dimension of the “architecture of the action.” Dramaturgy is also the name of a function in the German theatre system. In the latter case it stands for the department of a theatre in which the dramaturg works as well as for the intellectual authority which “dramaturgy” has over the invention and communication of theatre. Because of that, the work of a dramaturg is equally multifaceted: s/he belongs to the management of the theatre and is the creative director and curator of new teams and projects. A dramaturg also edits the literary source material of the play and is the ﬁrst observer of a new production next to the director. As such s/he can add his or her opinions and interpretations to the artistic process during the rehearsals. The important place of dramaturgy in the German-speaking theatre originates from its historical birth during the eighteenth century. Lessing’s Hamburg Dramaturgy (Hamburgische Dramaturgie) was instrumental for the self-reﬂection of theatre producers and a guide for the audience to acquaint it with the new art of bourgeois theatre. The emerging bourgeoisie in the politically tattered country saw itself as unﬁt to overthrow the traditional political relations in an act similar to the French Revolution. The unique path that Germany took was often described as an escape into the arts. The art of Romanticism and the German city theatre (Stadttheater) are the two most distinctive examples of this sublimation. During the nineteenth century every city tried to build a theatre in its centre as a sign of its self-conﬁdent citizens. The performances there were of varying quality and covered every genre: opera, operetta, ballet, play, musical comedy, melodrama, etc. The thriving market for plays oﬀered a range of diﬀerent texts, so the repertoire of the city theatre could satisfy the lust for entertainment and the wish for representation even-handedly. The birth of city theatre lies in the idealism of Lessing’s Dramaturgy, which was carried on by the dramaturgies of the theatre. People worked on and are still working on the idea of theatre as a political art of self-reﬂection. This idealism combines the philosophical and institutional dimensions of dramaturgy. At the beginning of this development stands the dramaturgy of the bourgeois tragedy (Bürgerliches Trauerspiel), which sought for a diﬀerent and new relation between the audience and the theatre, other than that of the folk theatre and the French tragedy, which provided either amusement or lofty elevation. A new dramaturgy of the action as much as a new dramaturgy of the performance was needed. The new characters had to show their inner lives, which led to a new dramaturgy of the psychological action. The characters knew about, and fought against, the constraints that social conventions imposed on them. The phantasm of the natural form was in the centre of this representation. Likewise, a new kind of acting had to be invented. To demonstrate the new situation believably, the actors had to learn to play in a new way. They had to be able to show the external constraints and the internal struggles at the same time, and they had to learn to play on two diﬀerent levels at once. The characters of psychological theatre feel and reﬂect their emotions; they are looking for something and are insecure whether this desire is right. They have to conceal something and nevertheless want to be acknowledged as individuals. The identiﬁcatory potential of the new theatre consists in the fact that the audience possesses the same technique of self-expression in their everyday lives. In civic society trust arises not through conventions of role-playing and the coding of the costume as it did at court, but by showing one’s inner, true, and therefore invisible personality. But how will someone be able to show these hidden qualities if their authenticity lies in the fact that they cannot be deliberately shown? Self-expression just has to happen, has to appear unintentionally and against the will of the subject. The border of desire and suﬀering, of feeling and thinking becomes the main diﬀerence in this bourgeois dramaturgy. This is why there is so much crying and sighing in the bourgeois tragedy. These borders of the sayable give an insight into the “true” self. In this way, the aspiring bourgeois class, which wanted to experience itself as true in its own feelings, found the adequate art for its self-discovery and self-aﬃrmation in the theatre. The subject of modern history is characterized by this self-reﬂection, which became the theme and the means of the presentation in the new dramaturgy of realism. During the nineteenth century, realism and naturalism brought this new method to perfection, which in turn had an impact on the art of acting. Until the reinvention of theatre as a bourgeois art, new inventions came from theatre authors and actors and originated from ritual and traditional sources. Now a new actor enters the stage. The new style of play desired by psychological realism necessitates rehearsals during which the new eﬀects of playing behind the “fourth wall” can be reviewed. The direct contact between actor and spectator is broken; the act of representation has to be invisible. Through this new kind of play, the audience disappears for the actor as much as for the spectator him or herself. S/he is not part of the audience anymore but the only one feeling in the dark stalls. The development of this new impression requires a surrogate for this lone spectator: the director enters the theatre. The director sits in the auditorium as a representative of every future member of the audience, and next to him or her sits the dramaturg as the ﬁrst critic of the event. From here, the handling of concentration, attention, and sympathy is organized. The dramaturgy of the action is staged with the dramaturgy of a performance. The theatre text does not become theatre within a convention or a tradition of a play, but every performance becomes an original production which bestows upon the text its own form of presentation. The goal of realistic theatre was the representation of bourgeois contradictions which originated in the necessary ambiguous communication between the market and alienated labour. Because capitalism turns everything into a commodity that receives its price on the market, life gets shaped by a double alienation of work on the one hand and the negotiation of prices on the other. As the new bourgeois class experiences itself as the winner of this alienation, the art of realism loses its critical potential and becomes a form of entertainment. The once dialectical representation of the world becomes “commercial realism,” which adopts the strong eﬀect of identiﬁcatory moments without the desire of showing the contradictions behind it. The enlightening power of realistic theatre loses itself in the lulling stream of feelings which eventually ends in the cinema. In the twentieth century, epic theatre turns against this tendency by taking the self- reference of the modern subject seriously. It re-establishes the contradiction as the foundation of a dialectical theatre. According to Brecht, the simplest deﬁnition of the epic manner of acting is the actor showing one thing while at the same time showing him or herself. By doing so, s/he establishes a relationship between showing and what is shown as well as between the one showing and the spectator. By this, the dispositive of the fourth wall gets abolished, the once direct contact, which characterized folk theatre, is established again and is expanded by the dimension of a reﬂecting actor. For dramaturgy, the epic theatre has far-ranging consequences. The architecture of the epic scene is diﬀerent from the dramatic situation insofar as it is no longer written to create suspense or a sense of identiﬁcation but for the act of showing. Likewise, the dramaturgy of a performance is no longer built towards a closed story arc (geschlossener Wirkungsbogen) but for the demonstration of certain aspects of the contradiction. The contradiction of the drama, which started the need for the characters to act, becomes the contradiction in society which the exemplary presentation shall make understandable by the exemplary presentation of speciﬁc facts. Therefore, the dramaturg’s collaboration during the rehearsals is no longer limited to aesthetic questions but broadens into the horizon of the social relevance of the theatrical event: how are the social contradictions reﬂected in human souls and bodies? The consequences of the political demand placed on theatre are hardly to be overemphasized for the German-speaking theatre system. They are connected to the enlightened idea of theatre as the art of an emancipated middle class as much as to the ideological feuds of the twentieth century. As a result of this, the dramaturg moves again to the center of the intermediation between theatre and reality. The rehearsals become enriched by his or her research, which subsequently becomes available for the audience in the form of the theatre program. The dramaturg’s vision, which is marked by the attitude of “include me out,” becomes the touchstone of social relevance. The art of epic theatre thereby frees itself from the desperate attempt of late bourgeois art to be meaningful because of the artist’s uniqueness, while rediscovering collective work as the natural state of theatre. The ramiﬁcations of psychological and epic theatre are similar for German theatre, but since the 1980s they have become increasingly overlaid by postmodern theory. This development operates under the name of the “postdramatic” but assembles numerous and sometimes contradictory characteristics of a postmodern theatre. Two manifestations of postdramatic theatre can be roughly distinguished. On the one hand, it stands in the tradition of visual arts, especially that of the early-twentieth-century avant-garde. This can be seen in the use of collages, which cause sensory and semantic eﬀects from the clash of unexpected materials. In this way, the dramaturgy of the performance no longer is structured by the dramatic action but by energetic, rhythmic, and other aesthetic phenomena. In this case, the dramaturg is not so much a mediator between the ﬁctional world of the drama, the reality of the performances, and the social presence as the co-author of a fable of the production that needs reinvention. Through the abandonment of the dramatic structure, the collective presence, as evoked by theatre, changes. One can say that dramatic theatre produces a community of feeling and identifying spectators whose presence is sentimental because it is directed backwards. On the other hand, epic theatre in contrast produces a community of astonished spectators, who come to know the familiar as strange in order to experience the changeability of the world as possible. Their present is coined by a faith in the future. The postdramatic theatre produces pictorial puzzles in which the audience can no longer decide whether what they are seeing is a sensual irritation or a semantic eﬀect, whether it is play or reality, whether it is meant or it really happens. This oscillation in perception generates a special form of presence. The self-reference of the modern subject, which is always experienced as a relation between at least two conﬂicting levels, becomes an aesthetical paradox of a selfreferent perception. Thus, the presence of perception becomes aware of itself and expands into a broader presence. One perceives and realizes one’s own perception at the same time. In this way, the broad presence lays itself over the past and the possible future. The oscillations of postdramatic theatre become a feast of self-referentiality in which the contradictions are no longer psychologically or socially justiﬁed but rather become aesthetic games. The other tendency of postdramatic theatre derives not so much from visual arts but from Brecht, to the extent that it could also be called post-epic theatre. Here, the play on two diﬀerent levels, as Brecht asked for, gets adopted, but without having recourse to the social position of the actor. It is no longer the political individual that tries to become aware of his or her class and, emancipated, stands in front of the audience, now the performer makes his or her own presence become the foundation of the stage presence. As a result, the techniques of realistic acting become mostly expendable because of the mimetic ability of creating a diﬀerent situation on stage so that the actual theatre situation is no longer necessary. The actor becomes a performer, which means that s/he enters the stage not as an acting subject but as one who is experiencing the world and reality. The performer is the always responsive employee that emotional capitalism demands. The dramaturgy of such a post-epic performance evolves from the scenic material which emerges during the rehearsals. There is no dramatic template from which the eﬀect and structure of the dramatic arc could be developed, but the scenic inventions must be composed by their diﬀerent dimensions. The dramaturgic assistance here becomes the central authority of artistic invention, requiring not only the techniques of drama but also the eﬀects of mash-ups, music, and dance, to arrange the speciﬁc material into something more than a scenic essay about a certain topic. The speciﬁc character of scenic inventions and the deliberate approach to them are part of postepic theatre. Because of this, the self-referentiality of the scene becomes central again, which previously – in its performative form – had its roots in performance art and in poststructuralism. During the performance, the scenic reality acquired an intrinsic value, because of self-referential plays and their continuity. Through this, the material emerges from behind the semiotic dimension. In poststructuralism, the sign becomes analyzed in view of its intrinsic value. Its power to signify something covers that which is hereby signiﬁed. Through the practice of such a deconstruction, all certainties crumble into discursive games. In a postmodern theatre that is critical towards representation, both techniques are often practiced. The categories of drama, mimesis, and catharsis as a banishment of spectators, who unite to form an audience in order to experience theatre as a collective, become replaced by the postmodern categories of self-reference, performance, and paradox. The diversity of the diﬀerent dramaturgic techniques is striking. In German theatre, all four traditions (dramatic, epic, postdramatic and post-epic) exist simultaneously, and the lines between oﬃcial city theatres and independent theatres become increasingly blurred. As a result, not only actors have to expand their skills. Above all, dramaturgy always has to invent and comprehend new architectures of actions and eﬀects. This variety of theatrical expressions has wide-ranging consequences for the education of young dramaturgs. There are two diﬀerent training routes in the German-speaking theatre. One runs through art colleges where dramaturgy is taught alongside acting, scenery, costume design, and directing. The other route is through theatre studies, which has diverse oﬀers in applied theatre studies. In this case, what is taught is not a speciﬁc skill but a theoretical understanding of theatre and theatrical events. As the foundation of applied theatre studies fell into the high phase of postmodern cultural theories, their aesthetic paradigms have been highly marked by them. The openness of the scientiﬁc education still dissociates itself from the classical, technical art forms of theatre and its mimetic claim. Applied theatre studies fosters a remarkable alliance of virtuosic perception, discursive processing, and production of new forms of theatre. The accusation that theatre is produced purely for theatre studies is certainly true for some of these self-referential formats. The production of more and more essay collections, which elevate a just-seen performance to the level of indispensable knowledge of the ﬁeld, surely fuels this cycle further. It cannot be overlooked that the innovative energy of the technical theatre education is in danger of weakening and that the forms inspired by these discourses frequently appear more modern and animated. Since public attention to theatre is rather diminishing, we have to ask whether this animosity is really useful, especially since this strong diﬀerentiation only furthers the exhaustion of mimetic energy and the encapsulation of postmodern aesthetics towards a complacent game. The prime task of the dramaturgs and dramaturgies is to build a connection between the dramatic art and the more discursive theatre. What is needed for this purpose is an intense engagement with the technical-mimetic side of theatre as much as with the discursive procedure. Such an engagement, however, has to break through the dividing barriers instead of getting entangled in more ﬁghts for distinction. And whose job would be more appropriate for this than that of the mediator, the dramaturg?

title: Forever Modernism
abstract: On or about April 2018, human character changed. At least it did at Coachella, when Beyoncé took the stage in all her majesty—as pan-African royalty, HBCU homecoming queen, pop icon, Southern heroine, and more—for two hours of brilliant spectacle and beautiful exertion. Whether it was as radical as the inspiration for Virginia Woolf's original declaration from 1910 that I stole shamelessly to start, Beyoncé's show definitely had more marching bands and better costumes. It was a performance that worked, and worked hard, on several registers at once, and explication in emoji started almost instantly on Twitter and beyond. From the aesthetics of black nationalism to the status of her marriage, Beyoncé was explicit and ambiguous at the same time, and even now—weeks later as I am writing, months later as you are reading—there is still more to say. “To address modernism,” writes Jed Rasula in History of a Shiver, “is to grapple with its endlessness, conceptually and materially if not temporally.” Or, as Craig Jenkins observed online the morning after, “We'll Revisit Beyonce's Coachella Performance for the Rest of Our Lives.”1 I will admit that this parallel began for me with the coincidence of an onrushing deadline and an irresistible distraction. But I want to take it further, and not simply because Beyoncé's show embodied so much of what Rasula terms the “maximal grandeur” of modernism in its totalizing aspirations, its attraction to the Gesamtkunstwerk (219). There are many lines of inquiry in History of a Shiver, and not all of them are best illuminated by reference to Beyoncé, which is almost certainly too small a slight for the Beyhive to notice. But any fan will recognize the unabashed and unironic ardor of Rasula's love for modernism, and though there are moments when his feelings get the best of his analysis, his book also reminds us why, from time to time, it is good that we are occasionally overwhelmed. Modernism, for Rasula, is the aesthetic and cultural history of the “intended big thing”; it retains a hold on us that is worth remembering, no matter where or when it finally happens and no matter what form it takes (21).Of course it feels a little strange to borrow Woolf's famous statement on her epoch to force the question of Beyoncé's “modernism,” and not just because Bloomsbury was one of the few places that we can all agree was even whiter than the audience at #Beychella. As shows of “impudence” go, to borrow from the full title of Rasula's History of a Shiver, I am being more ridiculous than sublime. And self-interested: at this point in its long history of innovation and exhaustion, modernism gets a lot more from a connection to Beyoncé than she does from it. Such a pairing is made stranger still considering History of a Shiver's noticeable silence on race in general and on modernism's particular indebtedness to African American culture. This absence limits the scope of Rasula's achievement, even if it often accurately reflects on the cramped horizons of his central figures despite the cultural reality they experienced. Yet Rasula has still written a commanding study of modernism that significantly expands our sense how it emerges and why it compels.
